name: Sneezing Face
baseMeaning: A yellow face with its eyes closed and a tissue held to its nose, mid-sneeze.
tldr: 🤧 says “I have a cold” or “I’m sneezing,” making it more specific than 🤒 for general illness.

contextMeanings.meaning: 🤧 directly reports that the sender is sneezing or has a cold.
🤧 serves as quick shorthand for “I’ve got a cold” without spelling out the symptoms.
contextMeanings.example: pretty sure it's just a cold 🤧

contextMeanings.meaning: When used while changing plans, 🤧 gives a practical health reason for postponing a date.
contextMeanings.example: i think i'm getting a cold, can we move saturday? 🤧

contextMeanings.meaning: In a work chat, 🤧 briefly explains why someone may be remote, absent, or working more slowly.
contextMeanings.example: i've got a cold, so i'm working from home today 🤧

platformNotes.note: In a one-to-one iMessage, 🤧 usually reports the sender’s own cold or sneezing fit. A short sentence gives the recipient context that a lone face cannot.
On Instagram, the emoji works in direct messages, captions, and comments where a visual symptom update fits. Because viewers may not know the sender, “cold” or “flu” in the caption removes ambiguity.
On TikTok, 🤧 can sit in a caption or comment as a quick illness update. The broad audience makes the surrounding sentence useful, particularly when the video itself is not about being sick.

In WhatsApp family or friend groups, 🤧 often explains why someone may be absent or quieter than usual. Group chats mix illness news with plans and pictures, so the emoji is easier to misread without text.

generationalNotes.note: Gen Z is likely to recognize 🤧 as casual shorthand for a cold and may send it alone in a relaxed chat. It does not appear to need a separate joke meaning.
Millennials are also likely to read 🤧 literally. When the illness is more serious, they may add a sentence such as “I’m home with the flu” so the tone is clear.
Gen X users will probably understand 🤧 without explanation, though some may prefer explicit wording in work or older family chats. Emoji habits vary more than the meaning does.

warnings.title: Using it for every illness
warnings.description: 🤧 suggests a cold or respiratory illness, while 🤒 is the better choice for vague or general unwellness. Sending 🤧 for fever, stomach trouble, or an unknown illness may narrow the meaning unintentionally.

warnings.title: Making recovery sound festive
warnings.description: Pairing 🤧 with 🎉, 🥳, 🎂, or other celebration symbols can turn a sickness update into a joke about the illness. Keep the message caring and specific instead.

seoDescription: What does 🤧 mean? It usually says “I have a cold” or “I’m sneezing,” and is more specific than the thermometer-face emoji for general illness.

longForm.overview:
🤧 travels easily from a private iMessage to a group WhatsApp thread or a work chat, but its meaning changes with the corner it lands in. The glyph shows a yellow face with closed eyes and a tissue pressed to its nose, so the immediate message is physical: someone is sneezing. That makes it more useful than the broader thermometer emoji 🤒 when a cold is the specific concern.

The main mistake is treating 🤧 as a catch-all for illness. People usually send it to mean “I have a cold” or “I’m sneezing,” while 🤒 better covers feeling generally unwell. A sentence still matters: 🤧 can report a respiratory illness, but it does not automatically explain whether the sender wants sympathy, a practical check-in, or simply an acknowledgment. In a friendly chat, the emoji may stand alone. In work, the same face becomes a brief status update. Near someone’s flu or stomach bug, it can work, but pairing it with a get-well message makes the intention clearer.
longForm.howPeopleUseIt:
🤧 shows up when someone reports a runny nose, a sudden sneezing fit, or a cold that is ruining their day. In a one-to-one chat, it may be the whole update: “still sneezing 🤧.” In a family group, it can explain why someone is skipping the gathering, though a sentence prevents relatives from treating the emoji as the full story.

The emoji saves people from describing symptoms in detail. “can’t stop sneezing 🤧” answers why someone is unavailable without becoming a medical report. With “I have a cold,” it confirms a respiratory illness rather than vague malaise. Around the flu, it can fit beside a get-well wish, but the words should show that this is a real illness update.
longForm.whenNotToUse:
Do not use 🤧 when you mean “I feel sick in general” and cannot identify a cold or sneezing. That is where 🤒 works better: it covers general illness, fever, or stomach trouble. Using 🤧 for every illness makes the message narrower, and a recipient may ask whether you have a cold.

Also keep it away from celebration. 🎉, 🥳, 🎂, and other festive symbols can turn a sickness update into a joke about the illness. If someone is reporting the flu or a stomach bug, use the sentence first and add 🤧 only when a respiratory illness fits. For concern without taking over, 😷 reads as supportive; 🫂 suggests a hug from a distance.
longForm.howToReply:
If someone sends 🤧, acknowledge the illness first: “feel better, rest up” or “take care of yourself.” You can add 🤧 to mirror what they sent, especially in a close chat where the exchange is already warm. A short reply is often enough; the emoji does not need a long explanation.

When someone is reporting flu or another bug, match their seriousness rather than turning the reply playful. A sentence such as “let me know if you need anything” shows support without assuming they want a joke. If 🤧 arrives under your own status update, reply with the useful detail they were probably asking for: whether you are resting, what you need, or when you expect to be back. If the emoji seems too vague, ask what they mean rather than guessing at the diagnosis.

faqs.question: What does 🤧 mean from a guy
faqs.answer: It usually means he is sneezing or has a cold. In a dating chat, it may explain why he is cancelling or postponing plans, but the emoji itself is not a sign of romantic interest.

faqs.question: Is 🤧 flirty
faqs.answer: No. 🤧 is a practical symptom update, not a flirty emoji. It can appear in a romantic conversation while someone is explaining a change of plans.

faqs.question: What does 🤧 mean on TikTok
faqs.answer: On TikTok, it normally means the sender has a cold or is sneezing. Add words when the caption or comment needs to distinguish a real illness update from a joke or a reaction.

faqs.question: Should I use 🤧 or 🤒 for a cold
faqs.answer: Use 🤧 for a specific cold or sneezing update. Use 🤒 when the problem is general illness without a clear respiratory cause.

conversationExamples.message: i think i'm coming down with a cold. can we move saturday? 🤧
conversationExamples.interpretation: They are giving a health reason for changing the date. Respond with concern and arrange another time instead of treating the emoji as romantic encouragement.

conversationExamples.message: my coworker gave me his cold and now i can't stop sneezing 🤧
conversationExamples.interpretation: They are reporting a contagious cold and probably venting about the inconvenience. Offer tissues, medicine, or space to rest and avoid joking about catching it.

conversationExamples.message: i've got a cold, so i'm staying home today to rest 🤧
conversationExamples.interpretation: This is a brief absence or remote-work update. Acknowledge it without pressuring the person to work or asking for unnecessary details about the illness.

conversationExamples.message: my little cousin has been sneezing all afternoon, send tissues please 🤧
conversationExamples.interpretation: They need practical family support for someone who may have caught a cold. A reply can offer supplies, check on the child, or suggest they rest and stay away from others.

conversationExamples.message: half the people at brunch are coughing, should we still go inside? 🤧
conversationExamples.interpretation: They are reporting possible illness around a group gathering and asking for advice. Respond by weighing the symptoms and considering a less crowded plan.
